title: Tightening the Iron Cage
text:
In the late 1980s, a small American manufacturer of circuit boards, which James Barker called ISE Communications, replaced its traditional hierarchy of supervisors with self-managing teams. Workers would now organize their own work, set their own schedules and hold each other accountable, guided by a shared statement of company values. Barker, a communication scholar, spent long periods at the plant observing meetings, interviewing workers and studying documents.

At first, the teams worked out their norms through discussion, grounded in shared values such as doing quality work and supporting each other. Over time, these norms hardened into formal rules. Teams set strict standards for attendance and punctuality and enforced them on each other, including on coworkers who had been friends. Members described the pressure from peers as much more intense than what they had felt under the old supervisors, because now their colleagues watched them all day and they felt they were letting the team down.

Barker called this concertive control: control that comes from workers themselves, based on shared values, rather than from managers. Borrowing an image from the sociologist Max Weber, he argued that removing the bosses had not freed the workers from the iron cage of bureaucratic control but had made it tighter.
lesson: Self-managed teams can police their members harder than any boss. Watch for peer pressure turning shared values into rigid rules.
location: A small manufacturing company in the United States
source: Barker, J. R. (1993). Tightening the iron cage: Concertive control in self-managing teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 38(3), 408-437.
